name: Drospirenone pill
lead: Drospirenone is a progestin and antiandrogen related to spironolactone, patented in 1976 by Schering AG and introduced as a combined pill with ethinylestradiol around 2000. It is sold as Yasmin, Yaz and generics, and is also used in progestin-only and estetrol combination pills.[1] Wikipedia notes the low-dose ethinylestradiol/drospirenone pill is indicated for moderate acne in some jurisdictions, alongside premenstrual disorders.[1]

Clinical research in the available sources centers on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where a systematic review compared drospirenone pills with other treatments.[2] Documented risks include venous thromboembolism and, with drospirenone, raised potassium.[1]

paras: Drospirenone pills are mainly contraceptives. Combined with ethinylestradiol, the pill is also indicated for moderate acne and premenstrual syndrome and dysphoric disorder.[1] Forms include drospirenone alone (Slynd), with ethinylestradiol (Yasmin, Yaz), with estetrol (Nextstellis) and with estradiol for menopause (Angeliq).[1]

Drospirenone antagonizes the androgen receptor at roughly 30 percent of the potency of cyproterone acetate in animals, which underlies its use for androgen-related skin symptoms.[1] It also blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor, offsetting estrogen-driven fluid retention, with about 3 to 4 mg said to be comparable to 20 to 25 mg of spironolactone in that effect.[1]

A 2017 systematic review of randomized trials in women with PCOS compared drospirenone pills with other standard treatments and reported that adding metformin was better than drospirenone alone for reducing BMI, among other findings.[2] An uncontrolled study of 51 Indian women with PCOS treated with ethinylestradiol 30 mcg plus drospirenone 3 mg followed them for up to twelve cycles.[3] Registered trials examine drospirenone-only pills for emergency contraception, after bariatric surgery, and in relation to blood pressure and vascular function.[4][5][6][7] These are not acne trials, and the sources reviewed did not include an acne-specific trial.

Ethinylestradiol-containing pills raise venous thromboembolism risk about fourfold, and some studies associate drospirenone pills with roughly 1.3 to 2.0 times the risk of levonorgestrel pills, though evidence is described as controversial and possibly confounded; Bayer has faced many lawsuits over the risk.[1] Drospirenone has potassium-sparing effects, and persistent hyperkalemia requiring discontinuation occurred in about 0.2 percent of women taking 4 mg alone.[1]

timeline.event: Introduced as a combined pill with ethinylestradiol.[1]

card.summary: An antiandrogenic birth-control progestin that is indicated for moderate acne in some regions, with most published research focused on PCOS.
card.note: Raises potassium and carries a venous clot risk; prescription only.

quick.overview:
Drospirenone is a progestin in contraceptive pills such as Yasmin and Yaz. Because it also blocks androgen receptors, the ethinylestradiol combination is indicated for moderate acne in some jurisdictions.

The studies in the sources reviewed are mostly in PCOS and contraception rather than acne itself.
quick.mechanism: It suppresses ovulation as a progestin, blocks androgen receptors, and blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor like spironolactone.
quick.risks: Combined pills raise clot risk; some studies suggest higher risk than levonorgestrel pills. Drospirenone can raise potassium. Prescription only.
